extracted.intended_audience: British statesmen, politicians, and the literate public concerned with the French Revolution (late 18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the legitimacy, effects, and prudence of political change (specifically the French Revolution) by examining institutions, fiscal policy, population, wealth, and civil society. Aimed at judging whether reform or total overthrow was warranted and what indicators reveal a government's health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population as a standard of government
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of a country's population is a certain standard for judging its government; 'No country in which population flourishes, and is in progressive improvement, can be under a very mischievous government.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use population size and growth (or decline, emigration, unemployment) as evidence for or against the claim that a government is destructive; Burke cites Intendants' estimates, Necker's figures, and contemporary emigration and unemployment (e.g., decline of Paris, 100,000 out of employment) as diagnostic facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wealth and economic indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: The wealth of a country — its bullion/specie, manufactures, agriculture, circulation, public works, ports, fortifications, and the condition of arts and charities — is a standard by which to judge whether a government protects or destroys prosperity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine coinage/specie records (Necker's mint figures), circulation of money, quality of manufactures and agriculture, infrastructure (roads, bridges, canals, ports), naval and military apparatus, and the flourishing of arts and institutions as evidence against exaggerated claims of despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for property, credit, and liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: A government's respect for property rights, public credit, and individual liberty is central to its legitimacy; violent outrages on credit, property, and liberty (e.g., compulsory paper currency and confiscation) are grave signs of misrule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for measures like compulsory paper currency, confiscation of estates, and arbitrary financial innovations that undermine credit and property; Burke calls compulsory paper currency an 'outrage upon credit, property, and liberty' and warns of the alliance of bankruptcy and tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness of fiscal policy and public finance
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiscal measures must avoid sudden shocks (e.g., immediate wholesale sale of Church lands) and reckless creation of paper money or debt; poor financial design will depress values and wreck circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proposals for land sales, exchange of stock, creation of new debt (three percent loan), and issuance of paper currency founded on eventual land sales. Burke explains how immediate mass sale would depress land values, divert circulating money to land, and how issuing paper to satisfy bank demands inflates fictitious wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of the judiciary and separation from executive power
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserving an independent judicature (Parliaments/magistrates) prevents consolidation of arbitrary power; abolishing independent courts cuts off a check on dictatorial centralization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the consequences of abolishing courts even if they had faults; Burke notes magistrates 'had purchased their places' but argues abolition removes a locus to which people might resort and enables rulers in Paris to demand implicit obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of minorities against majority tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure democracy risks subjecting minorities to severe oppression by a majority; a majority in a democracy can exercise crueller persecution of a minority than a single despot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate regimes for safeguards that prevent majoritarian persecution. Burke emphasizes that oppression by multitudes leaves sufferers without consolation and can be more furious and extensive than princely tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of a mixed constitution (moderation and balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tempered or mixed government — monarchy directed by laws, balanced by hereditary wealth and dignity, and checked by popular organs — is preferable to the extremes of absolute monarchy or pure democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge proposals for government by asking whether they preserve reciprocal control among institutions and whether reforms can ingraft republican elements onto monarchy more easily than the reverse (cites Bolingbroke's observation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for measured reform over wholesale destruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where abuses exist, measured reform (improving existing institutions) is preferable to leveling the whole fabric of government by violent revolution; initial popular instructions sought reform, not destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between grievances that can be corrected and those warranting total overthrow. Burke warns that people are sometimes hurried into things they would have rejected if they had seen the whole together; he stresses examining whether former government was reformable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil society and cultural indicators as evidence of regime quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence and flourishing of literature, philosophy, arts, learned men, charities, and public institutions indicate a government that is not wholly destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the richness of civil society — philosophers, critics, historians, poets, orators, public charity, learned institutions — alongside material indicators to judge whether claims of despotism are justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior and social role of the nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: The conduct of the nobility — their private behavior toward inferiors, their hospitality, military tone, and local civil role — should be assessed before condemning an estate as wholly oppressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid caricaturing a class; Burke argues many French nobles were well-bred, humane, and not systemically oppressive, and were not primarily responsible for the most grievous revenue abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating vested interests in plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the spoil of institutions (e.g., Church lands) as the vital resource of state operations and forcing citizens to partake (via compulsory paper) binds citizens to uphold sacrilegious acts by creating a guilty shared interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for policies that make the new regime's survival depend on public complicity in plunder (forcing circulation of depreciated paper), thereby corrupting civic incentives and consolidating power by self-interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against rapid market flooding of real property
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden introduction of a vast quantity of landed property to market will depress land values and harm the landed interest and overall economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate plans for land disposal for their macroeconomic effects; Burke explains that immediate mass sale would depreciate the value of all landed estates and shift circulating money away from trade into land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness of compensation and the real worth of payments
rubrics_metrics.description: Compensation paid in depreciated or speculative paper (rather than real value) is unjust and undermines the legitimacy of settlement for displaced officials or holders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize proposals that convert real property or purchased offices into claims paid in depreciated currency or paper stock; Burke notes lawyers and dismissed magistrates were to be 'compensated' in paper that bore 'the indelible character of sacrilege.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of exploitation by purchasers granted deferred or precarious tenure
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting estates to purchasers who pay only a portion (deferred payment) and who hold under precarious political tenure incentivizes waste, extortion of peasants, and dismantling of estate value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tenure terms: deferred payment and precarious settlement create incentives to extract value immediately (selling building materials, wasting woods) and to burden tenants to meet obligations, rather than preserving productive estate use.
